chunks: Why prefer non-inverting op-amp stages. The question: Why are non-inverting configurations often preferred?
An op-amp is a chip that amplifies the difference between its two inputs, plus and minus.
A stage adds resistors that feed part of the output back to the minus input to set the gain. There are two ways to wire it.
In the non-inverting way, the signal goes straight into the plus input and the output has the same sign.
In the inverting way, the signal goes through a resistor into the minus input and the output flips sign.
Most of the time you prefer the non-inverting way because it barely loads whatever feeds it.
Think of reading the level in a water tank. A clear glass gauge on the side lets you see the level without taking any water out. That is the non-inverting input.
A pipe that drains water out of the tank to measure it is the inverting input: you change the tank by measuring it.
This only matters for a weak source: a huge lake barely notices a small drain.
In (a) the sensor drives the high-impedance + input and the buffer follows it.
In (b) the same sensor drives R in into a virtual ground, so its 10 kilohms simply adds to R in and the gain is cut in half.
Input impedance: how hard it is for current to flow into an input. Higher means the input takes less current and disturbs the source less.
Source resistance: the resistance inside the thing driving the input, such as a sensor. Gain: output voltage divided by input voltage.
Op-amp: see "What an op-amp is and how it works". The two circuits are compared in "Inverting and non-inverting op-amp circuits".
A sensor puts out 1 volts and has 10 kilohms of resistance inside. Feed it into an inverting stage with a 10 kilohms input resistor.
The sensor's own 10 kilohms adds to that resistor, so the gain is cut in half, as if only 0. 5 volts had arrived. Now feed it into the plus input of a non-inverting stage.
That input draws almost no current, so nearly the full 1 volts arrives. That is the whole idea.
"Non-inverting stages are often preferred because the input goes straight into the op-amp's high-impedance plus terminal, so they don't load the source or turn its resistance into a gain error.
They also don't invert, can be built as a unity-gain buffer, and for the same signal gain have slightly better bandwidth.
The downsides: the gain is at least one, and both inputs swing with the signal, so common-mode range and CMRR matter.
For summing or low-impedance sources, the inverting stage is just as good."
